Shelta is a cant language, a type of secret language used by traveling people and traditionally by Irish Travellers. It is also known as the Gammon, the Irish Travellers' Language, and the Cant.

Phonology
Shelta has a number of unusual phonological features. One of these is the use of a letter /ꭕ/ which represents a voiceless velar fricative, a sound that is similar to the Scottish "ch" in "loch" but is produced further back in the mouth. This sound is held for a longer duration than other consonants in the language. Another feature is the use of vowel length, where the length of a vowel can change the meaning of a word. For example, the word "doll" can mean 'world' or 'pig' depending on the length of the vowel.

Morphology and Syntax
Shelta has a complex morphological system, with many words being made up of a root word and various affixes. For example, the word "skraꭕo" for 'tree, bush' contains the consonant /ꭕ/, which is a hissing sound that is held in the back of the throat and is held longer than other consonants.

Loanwords
Some Shelta words have been borrowed by mainstream English speakers, such as the word "bloke" meaning 'a man' in the mid-19th century.

Orthography
There is no standard orthography for Shelta. Broadly speaking, Shelta can either be written following an Irish-type orthography or an English-type orthography. For example, the word for 'married' can either be spelled lósped or lohsped; the word for 'woman' can either be spelled beoir or byohr.
